strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and under-explored problem: instruction-based editing of images beyond the native resolution of pretrained diffusion models (>1K), and the proposed formulation (edit at low resolution, then transfer fine-grained source details at high resolution via patch-wise test-time optimization) is a sensible and clearly motivated decomposition of the task.

The technical design is well reasoned: the adaptive feature-space transfer function (learnable 1x1 convolution on intermediate U-Net/DiT features, Eq. 8) is a lightweight and spatially adaptive alternative to a global constant vector, and the authors empirically motivate this design choice over a constant parameterization.

The patch synchronization mechanism (blended Tweedie estimates over auxiliary boundary latents plus a resampling strategy, Secs. 4.5.1-4.5.2) avoids the overlapping-inference window common in tiled diffusion methods, which is a genuine efficiency contribution; the ablation (Figs. 5a, 7) qualitatively demonstrates reduced boundary artifacts.

The method is shown to generalize across backbones (U-Net-based Stable Diffusion 2.1 and transformer-based FLUX.1-dev), and the appendix provides pseudo-code, layer-selection details, and additional ablations (hyperparameter tau), supporting reproducibility of the pipeline.

The masked metric protocol (M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR via LANG-SAM masks) is a thoughtful attempt to separately measure preservation of regions intended to remain unchanged, and the comparison against four recent diffusion-based SR baselines (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR) shows consistent, if moderate, quantitative gains (Table 1).
weaknesses: The evaluation is built entirely on a self-constructed benchmark of AI-generated images (FreeScale 4K synthesis downsampled to 2K/1K/512), which are stylized/fantasy-like rather than natural photographs. This narrows the claimed scope of 'high-resolution image editing' and may favor the method; there is no evaluation on real high-resolution photographs, which is the primary practical use case.

The baseline set is narrow. The only comparison is the edit-then-SR pipeline (NanoBanana + SR). Alternative direct high-resolution strategies — tiled/MultiDiffusion-style editing, hierarchical approaches (DemoFusion, ScaleCrafter), SDEdit at higher resolution with downsampled conditioning, or simply applying the low-res editor per-patch with any seam-blending — are neither compared nor empirically ruled out, leaving the strong claim of state-of-the-art under-supported.

The claim of being 'the first to propose the high-resolution image editing task' is overstated; tiled/hierarchical diffusion editing of large images has been explored in the high-resolution generation literature, and the related-work discussion does not seriously engage with these as editing alternatives.

The evaluation protocol is ambiguous on a key point: PSNR/SSIM/MSE must be computed against some reference target, but no ground-truth high-resolution edited image exists. It appears the low-resolution NanoBanana edit serves as the implicit target, which would mean the metrics partially reward reproducing the reference rather than measuring instruction fidelity; no instruction-following metric (e.g., CLIP-based) or user study is provided to verify that edits are actually semantically executed at high resolution.

There is an internal inconsistency regarding the key hyperparameter tau: Section 5.1 states tau = 15 is used, while the appendix ablation (Table 2) reports tau = 35 as the default/best setting. Additionally, Sec. 4.4 defines tau via 'Delta_h_t = 0 for all t >= tau' while Algorithm 1 applies optimization for t < tau, creating confusion about whether the transfer is active at early or late timesteps.

No runtime, memory, or optimization-cost analysis is reported despite the method being a per-patch, per-timestep test-time optimization (with optional Null-text inversion and a resampling step that doubles forward passes). The claimed computational advantage over overlapping inference remains unsubstantiated quantitatively.

Quantitative margins are small in absolute terms (e.g., HaarPSI 0.342 vs 0.335; M-PSNR ~22.1 vs ~21.5), and statistical significance/variance over the 400 samples is not reported. The ablation of the constant-vector vs 1x1-conv transfer function is anecdotal ('cat-to-dog' failure) rather than quantified.

The method inherits artifacts from the low-resolution editor (acknowledged in Limitations), and since the text instruction is only applied indirectly through the low-res reference (the diffusion process itself uses an empty prompt), edit strength at high resolution is entirely dependent on an external commercial model (Gemini/NanoBanana), which weakens reproducibility and self-containment of the contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (editing beyond the native operating resolution of pretrained diffusion editors) and the proposed pipeline—patch-wise test-time optimization of a feature-space transfer function plus a non-overlapping synchronization mechanism—is technically coherent and clearly described, with pseudo-code and implementation details supporting reproducibility.

The synchronization design is a sensible contribution: the blended-Tweedie auxiliary latent plus the resampling strategy (Eq. 13-14) decouples synchronization from detail injection and avoids costly overlapping inference, which is a meaningful efficiency argument compared to MultiDiffusion/DemoFusion-style overlap sampling.

The method is shown to generalize across backbones (SD 2.1 U-Net and FLUX.1-dev), and ablations on the synchronization module (Fig. 5a, Fig. 7) and on the timestep hyperparameter τ (Table 2) are provided, with a plausible rationale for the adaptive 1x1-conv transfer function over a global constant vector.
The masked metric protocol (LANG-SAM-derived foreground/background masks for M-MSE/M-SSIM/M-PSNR) is a thoughtful attempt to quantify preservation of regions intended to remain unchanged.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not actually measure editing quality. All reported metrics (M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR, HaarPSI) are computed against the source image to quantify preservation, but there is no ground truth for the edit itself and no metric of instruction following or fidelity to the intended edit (e.g., CLIP-based edit-alignment, similarity to the low-res reference, or a user study). A method that makes overly conservative edits would score well on all reported metrics, so Table 1 only supports half of the paper's claim.

Baselines are limited to a single edit-then-SR pipeline (NanoBanana + four SR models). No comparison against the many other plausible approaches: joint multi-patch editing with MultiDiffusion-style fusion, DemoFusion/FreeScale-style edited generation at high resolution, direct high-resolution editing via modified attention (ScaleCrafter/HiDiffusion-style), or simply applying SD-xl/FLUX-based editors at 2K. The claim of state-of-the-art is only established against one family of alternatives.

The benchmark is entirely synthetic and small: 400 pairs where sources are themselves FreeScale-generated 4K AI images, edited with a single commercial model (NanoBanana). There are no real photographs, no diversity analysis, and no human evaluation, which is essential for a perceptual editing task where the qualitative gains claimed (Fig. 4) are subtle.

There is an internal inconsistency on a core hyperparameter: Section 5.1 states 'we use ... hyperparameter τ = 15' as the default, while Appendix D reports that 'the default setting τ = 35 achieves the best performance across all metrics' and Table 2 shows τ=35 is best. This undermines confidence in the experimental reporting.

Test-time optimization cost is significant—per-patch, per-timestep optimization of the transfer function, forward trajectories for three image sets, plus resampling and auxiliary latent passes—yet no runtime, memory, or compute comparison to the edit-then-SR baselines is given, despite the paper advertising computational efficiency as a selling point.

The novelty claim ('first to propose the high-resolution image editing task') is overstated; patch-wise diffusion at high resolutions with boundary harmonization is well explored (MultiDiffusion, DemoFusion, ScaleCrafter), and feature-injection during inversion-based editing is closely related to PnP/Null-text-based methods. The paper is best viewed as an incremental combination of these ideas applied to a new setting.

Quantitative margins in Table 1 are modest (e.g., HaarPSI 0.342 vs 0.335, M-PSNR 22.114 vs 21.519) and no statistical significance or variance across the 400 pairs is reported; with a single seed and no user study, the practical significance is unclear.

Several technical details are under-specified: the choice of which U-Net/transformer layers receive the transfer function is deferred to a brief appendix note, the interaction between the blended-Tweedie update (Eq. 14) and the resampled noise term is not analyzed for correctness, and the behavior for large semantic changes between source and reference (where a 1x1-conv per-patch transfer function is learned from only ~35 timesteps) is not studied quantitatively.

strengths: Introduces a practically relevant and clearly motivated task — high-resolution image editing — and frames the central challenge (transferring fine-grained source details into an edited result produced at low resolution) in a convincing way.

Proposes a training-free, test-time optimization framework with a well-motivated design: a learnable 1x1-convolution transfer function in the feature space of a frozen diffusion model, plus a blended-Tweedie synchronization mechanism that avoids overlapping-patch inference, which is a sensible efficiency-oriented contribution.
The method is backbone-agnostic in spirit: results are shown for both U-Net-based Stable Diffusion 2.1 and transformer-based FLUX.1-dev, supporting generality claims.

The paper is generally well organized; the method is formalized precisely (Eqs. 1-14), pseudo-code (Algorithm 1), detailed synchronization formulas, layer-selection strategy, hyperparameter (τ) ablation, limitations, and societal impact are provided, which aids reproducibility of the described procedure.
Ablation results (Fig. 5, 7) visually demonstrate that the synchronization strategy meaningfully reduces patch-boundary artifacts relative to naive independent patch denoising.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation relies exclusively on fidelity-style metrics (M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR, HaarPSI) computed against the source image. These metrics reward preservation of source content but provide no evidence of edit quality or instruction following. A method that closely copies the source would score well on all four metrics. There is no LPIPS/CLIP-directional similarity, no user study, and no metric measuring semantic alignment with the editing instruction, so the central claim of 'state-of-the-art editing capacity' is only partially supported.

All baselines are of a single family (edit-then-super-resolve with NanoBanana + four SR models). Missing comparisons include: directly running the editing model on the 2K input, patch-wise naive direct editing at high resolution, multiband/latent fusion combinations of the edited low-res image with the high-res source, and high-resolution generation-editing hybrids (e.g., ScaleCrafter/FreeScale-style pipelines applied to editing). Without these, it is hard to judge whether the full test-time-optimization machinery is necessary.

The evaluation data is entirely synthetic: sources are generated by FreeScale, edits by NanoBanana, instructions by ChatGPT. There are no real photographs, and the edited 512²/1K references are never observed at high resolution, so the benchmark cannot capture failures on real-world content or diverse texture statistics. The claim of being 'the first to propose the high-resolution image editing task' is also likely overclaimed given prior work touching editing beyond 1K, and no related-work discussion substantiates the novelty claim rigorously.

Computational cost is a selling point ('does not require overlapping inference, effectively decreasing the computational demand') yet no runtime, memory, or FLOP comparison to any baseline (including overlapping-patch synchronization) is reported. Test-time optimization per patch, per timestep is presumably expensive; the absence of any cost analysis is a material gap.

The ablation on the transfer function design (constant vector vs. 1x1 conv) is only qualitative ('we observe that it fails'), with no numbers, and the τ ablation covers only three values on a 60-pair subset. Additional component-level ablations (e.g., effect of Null-text inversion, choice of injection layers) are absent or relegated to qualitative statements.

Some technical inconsistencies reduce clarity: the definition of τ (transfer applied for t < τ, so Δh = 0 for t ≥ τ) is stated confusingly and interacts oddly with the interpolation weight M(v,t) = (2v/Hp)(1 − t/τ); Figure 2's caption states ˜y0[i] = y_high0[i], which contradicts the goal of producing an edited output rather than reconstructing the source; the blended-estimate notation L(·) in the main text (Sec. 4.5.1) does not match the operator-plus-mask form given in the appendix (Eq. 19/22), where Eq. 22 also appears to use incorrect operands.

No code release is mentioned, and the pipeline depends on Null-text inversion plus per-image optimization, which makes exact reproduction costly; combined with the synthetic benchmark, reproducibility of the reported comparison is limited.

Qualitative evidence for detail transfer is largely on AI-generated, texture-rich fantasy images; several figures (e.g., sky/cloud crops in Fig. 7) show only subtle differences between 'w/o Sync' and 'Ours', and no quantitative artifact metric for synchronization is provided beyond the global fidelity table.

strengths: The paper introduces a clearly motivated and practically relevant task — instruction-based editing beyond the ~1K operating range of current editing models — and frames it in a way that decouples semantic editing (low-res reference) from fine-detail transfer (high-res source), which is a sensible decomposition.

The technical approach is well-articulated: a test-time-optimized, timestep-dependent 1x1-conv feature transfer function aligned between low-res and high-res diffusion trajectories (Sec. 4.4), plus a synchronization mechanism (blended Tweedie estimates with resampling, Sec. 4.5) that avoids overlapping inference. The auxiliary-latent blending and the resampling trick that decouples synchronization from detail injection are non-trivial and thoughtfully designed.

The method is architecture-agnostic in spirit: it is demonstrated on both U-Net-based Stable Diffusion v2.1 and the transformer-based FLUX.1-dev, with the necessary flow-matching adaptations (Eqs. 23-27) described in the appendix, and scales to 8K-editing.

Supplementary material is strong: pseudo-code (Algorithm 1), exact synchronization formulas (Eqs. 15-22), ablations on the timestep hyperparameter τ, on the placement/design of the transfer module (Table 3), an ablation of synchronization (Fig. 9), real-image experiments (Fig. 7, Table 4), and an honest discussion of computational cost and limitations.

Quantitative results (Table 1, Table 4) show consistent, if moderate, improvements over all four SR-based baselines across both 1K and 2K scenarios on five metrics, including masked variants designed to measure preservation of unedited regions.
weaknesses: The evaluation is built entirely on a self-constructed benchmark: 100 synthetic sources generated by FreeScale at 4K, with instructions authored by ChatGPT and references produced by Nano Banana. There is no public benchmark, no user study, and no direct perceptual/semantic evaluation of edit faithfulness in the main comparison. Given the task is new, a human evaluation would substantially strengthen the claim of 'high-quality edits'.

The baseline family is narrow. All four baselines are 'edit-then-super-resolve' pipelines. Obvious alternative strategies — tiled/patch-wise editing approaches (e.g., MultiDiffusion/SyncDiffusion-style synchronization applied to editing), high-res-capable editing models, or directly patch-wise running an editing model — are not compared, making it hard to judge whether the proposed test-time optimization is genuinely the right machinery versus simply the only alternative tested.

Quantitative margins over the strongest baselines are modest (e.g., HaarPSI 0.342 vs. 0.335; M-PSNR 22.132 vs. 21.528 in 1K), and some comparisons are somewhat structurally favored: SR baselines never see the high-res source, so masked preservation metrics will almost necessarily favor a method that directly conditions on it. LPIPS between source and target conflates detail preservation with degree of editing.

The method requires per-image, per-timestep, per-patch test-time optimization: 234.77s without NTI and 635.51s with NTI on a single A6000, versus 0.74-88.06s for baselines, and it runs in full precision (20.29 GB) for numerical stability. This is a large practical gap that limits usefulness, and the claimed future half-precision fix is speculative.

Reliance on Nano Banana (a proprietary model) for reference generation limits reproducibility of the benchmark, and the acknowledged artifact-propagation limitation (Sec. H) is potentially significant since the whole pipeline inherits the reference's errors.

The central empirical claim about the transfer function — that it injects fine-grained detail without destroying edit semantics — is supported only weakly: Table 3 shows CLIP-Sim differences between design choices of ~0.0001-0.003, which is near noise; the semantics-vs-detail trade-off of the constant-vs-convolutional variant (the motivation for Eq. 8) is asserted from qualitative observation rather than demonstrated quantitatively.

The 'first to propose high-resolution image editing' claim is stated strongly; given the existence of tiled latent diffusion techniques and high-res restoration/editing hybrids, this novelty claim should be more carefully qualified.

The synchronization section describes only pairwise vertical blending between adjacent patches; handling of 2x2 patch corners and junction consistency is deferred to the appendix and not analyzed, and no quantitative ablation of synchronization (only visual) is provided in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practical gap: existing instruction-based editing methods (Step1X-Edit, ICEdit, KV-Edit) are limited to ~1K resolution, and the naive edit-then-super-resolve pipeline demonstrably fails to carry over fine source textures. Formalizing high-resolution editing and providing a benchmark protocol (masked MSE/SSIM/PSNR, LPIPS, HaarPSI with instruction-aware LANG-SAM masks) is a useful contribution to the community.

The technical approach is sensible and clearly motivated: patch-wise inference keeps the pretrained model within its native resolution, a timestep-dependent, spatially-adaptive 1x1-conv transfer function injects source detail during the reverse trajectory, and a blended-Tweedie synchronization with a resampling strategy avoids overlapping-inference costs. The design is well-motivated (e.g., the argument for adaptive vs. constant transfer functions in Sec. 4.4).

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive for a first paper on this task: 1K- and 2K-editing scenarios, four diffusion-SR baselines, qualitative comparisons with zoomed crops, an ablation on synchronization (Fig. 5a, Fig. 9), hyperparameter ablation on τ (Table 2), module placement ablation (Table 3), generalization to FLUX.1-dev, 8K demonstration, real-image experiments on 285 Pexels pairs (Table 4), and a computational cost discussion (Appendix G).
Limitations are honestly acknowledged (artifact propagation from the low-res editor, reliance on pretrained model quality, full-precision requirement and high runtime).
weaknesses: Evaluation is dominated by synthetic, AI-generated content: the main benchmark (100 sources, 400 pairs per scenario) is created by FreeScale + ChatGPT prompts, and references are produced by Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5), a closed-source commercial model. This raises both distribution-validity concerns (results may not transfer to natural photographs, where reconstructions via Null-text inversion and patch-level detail transfer are harder) and reproducibility concerns, since the reference images central to the pipeline and benchmark cannot be regenerated. The real-image subset (285 pairs) is relegated to the supplement with no corresponding 2K results.

There are troubling metric inconsistencies that undermine trust in the quantitative claims: LPIPS is reported around 0.46-0.51 in Table 1, but 0.16-0.19 in Table 3 (ablations, 60 pairs) and 0.13-0.14 in Table 4 (real images) for what appear to be the same metric and broadly similar task. Either the evaluation protocol differs silently between tables or there is an error; the paper does not explain this three-fold discrepancy. HaarPSI (~0.33 in Table 1 vs ~0.37 in Table 4) shows a smaller but similar pattern. These inconsistencies need clarification before the SOTA claim can be fully credited.

The baseline set is narrow. The only comparison is against edit-then-SR pipelines built on Nano Banana. Plausible alternatives are absent: directly running a strong open editor on 1K/2K inputs (e.g., Step1X-Edit at its native capability), patch-wise application of a diffusion editor (MultiDiffusion-style), or SR methods conditioned on the high-resolution source (some Real-ISR methods accept image conditioning, which would weaken the 'source details are not conditioned' argument). Without these, the claimed advantage of the proposed framework over simpler strategies is not fully established.

The claim of being 'first to propose high-resolution image editing' is overstated; patch-wise/tiled editing, high-resolution inpainting, and resolution-extrapolating editing variants exist in adjacent literature, and the paper should temper this claim and position itself against that line of work.

Cost is substantial and asymmetrically reported: 234.77s (635.51s with NTI) and 20.29 GB in full precision versus baselines at 0.74-88.06s and 8.40-36.00 GB. The suggestion that half-precision 'is anticipated' to work is unverified. For a test-time optimization method operating over N x M patches, per-image cost scaling with resolution (8K results) is not quantified.

No user study is provided despite the task being perceptual and the masked-metric protocol (built on LANG-SAM masks and downsampled GT) being debatable as a proxy for edit quality; e.g., a method could score well on M-PSNR while failing instruction semantics. CLIP-Sim is used only in one ablation, not in the main comparison. Also, the synchronization ablation is purely qualitative (boundary artifacts), with no metric quantifying seam severity.

Several methodological details are thin: the transfer function is optimized independently per patch and per timestep against the high-res source trajectory, yet synchronization is only applied for t <= τ; interactions between per-patch optimization drift and the blending are not analyzed. Eq. (12)'s interpolation weight couples spatial blending strength to the timestep in a way that is asserted rather than justified. The appendix resampling argument (Eq. 13) preserves injected detail implicitly but provides no analysis of detail retention across the forward-resample.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and relatively underexplored problem: instruction-based editing of images at 1K+ resolutions where existing editors (Step1X-Edit, ICEdit, KV-Edit) fail. Framing high-res editing as detail transfer from a high-res source into a low-res edited reference is a sensible and clearly articulated insight.

The method is technically coherent: a per-patch, timestep-dependent 1x1-conv transfer function optimized via trajectory alignment (Eq. 6), combined with a blended-Tweedie synchronization that avoids overlapping-tile inference (Eq. 12-14) is a clean design, and the resampling trick (Sec. 4.5.2) that decouples synchronization from detail injection is a nice solution to a real problem.

The evaluation is reasonably thorough for a first paper on this task: 400 evaluation pairs per scenario, masked metrics designed to measure preservation of unchanged regions, both synthetic (FreeScale-generated) and real (Pexels) test sets, ablations on tau and on the choice of layer/design of the transfer function, and generalization to a flow-matching backbone (FLUX.1-dev).
Consistent quantitative gains over all four SR-pipeline baselines on both 1K- and 2K-editing (Table 1, Table 4), and the computational cost discussion in the appendix is candid rather than hidden.
The manuscript is well written and well organized; the supplementary material includes pseudo-code, full synchronization formulas, and FLUX adaptation details, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The baseline set is narrow. The only comparison is 'edit at low resolution + diffusion SR'. Missing baselines include: (i) running existing editors at higher but still feasible resolutions (e.g., SDXL/FLUX editing at 1K, hierarchical/tiled editing with MultiDiffusion-style latent blending), (ii) patch-wise editing with existing synchronization methods (the paper claims its sync avoids overlapping inference, but never quantifies the quality/cost gap against overlap-based synchronization), and (iii) FreeScale-style architectural scaling applied to the editor. Without these, the claim of state-of-the-art high-res editing is only established against the weakest family of alternatives.

The test-time cost is significant and only partially acknowledged: 234.77s (or 635.51s with NTI) and ~20GB VRAM per 1K image versus 0.74-88s for baselines, plus forward/reverse inversion of all N x M patches. This is a material limitation for the stated use case ('users seek precise modifications'), and no user study is provided to justify whether the quality gain is worth an order-of-magnitude runtime increase.

The benchmark is self-constructed: 100 source images generated by FreeScale, prompts/instructions from ChatGPT, and references produced by Nano Banana (a closed-source commercial model). This raises reproducibility and generalization concerns, and the dependence on a proprietary black-box editor makes the pipeline hard to reproduce exactly. The public benchmarking of the task would be stronger with an established dataset.

Metric concerns: LPIPS is computed between source and target images, which rewards preservation but penalizes the intended edit itself; combined with masked metrics computed with LANG-SAM masks, the evaluation is largely a faithfulness-to-source measure. Edit-quality or instruction-following is only weakly covered (a single CLIP-Sim ablation). The large discrepancy in LPIPS between Table 1 (~0.46-0.50) and Table 4 (~0.13-0.15) is not explained.

The claim of being 'the first to propose the high-resolution image editing task' is overstated; patch-wise diffusion with latent blending for high-res synthesis/editing has substantial precedent (MultiDiffusion, Mixture of Diffusers, DemoFusion, FreeScale itself), and high-res editing via tiled strategies has been explored in community/practice. The novelty is better positioned as an incremental but well-executed combination of test-time trajectory alignment and non-overlapping synchronization.

The synchronization ablation is primarily qualitative (Figure 5a, Figure 9); a quantitative boundary-consistency metric or user study would substantiate the claim that blended-Tweedie synchronization reduces artifacts. The gain of the method over baselines is also modest in absolute terms on several metrics (e.g., HaarPSI 0.342 vs 0.335), so stronger statistical or perceptual evidence would strengthen the case.

Minor: several baseline SR methods are one-step distilled models designed for degraded inputs; applying them to Nano-Banana-edited images may not represent their best configuration. Also, editing with an empty prompt for all patches is surprising given the semantic gap between patches and deserves more analysis.
